title: Build an agent that finds where work gets stuck
description: A system that reads your tracker's timestamp data and ranks the process stages costing you the most time.

diff.title: Diff
diff.content: A side-by-side view of what changed between two versions of a file. Red lines were removed, green lines were added. When Claude shows you a diff, it's previewing exactly what's about to change before you approve.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

handoff.title: Handoff
handoff.content: When your main agent passes a job to a sub-agent and waits for the result. Cleaner than mixing two agents' contexts in one thread, and the moment to inspect for prompt injection if either agent is reading untrusted input.

batch-api.title: Batch API
batch-api.content: A way to send a big pile of requests to Claude at once and get the results back later (usually within 24 hours) at a discount. Good for one-time bulk jobs like classifying 10,000 customer support tickets.

automation.title: Automation
automation.content: Having Claude run tasks automatically on a schedule or trigger — without you manually starting them each time. For example, checking your inbox every morning and summarizing it to Slack.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Most teams already have the data that would show them where work stalls. It just sits in a tracker instead of getting analyzed. [Deloitte's 2025 Global Process Mining Survey](https://www.deloitte.com/de/de/services/consulting-financial/research/global-process-mining-survey.html) found 25% of organizations already use AI within their process mining work, with 74% planning to add it within two years.

Task and process-level event data, timestamps, stage changes, ticket history, is the same input that reveals bottlenecks, delays, and manual [handoffs](#tooltip-handoff) ripe for [automation](#tooltip-automation). This system reads an export of that data, calculates time-in-stage for every item, and ranks the stages costing you the most time, with the numbers behind each one.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) whenever throughput feels off, a saved skill for a recurring check, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that reruns monthly and [diffs](#tooltip-diff) against the last pass.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your process, your data export, your lookback window, and what counts as a stall.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that looks at our ticket or task data and tells me where our [process name] actually gets stuck instead of guessing. Ask me questions, one at a time, about the process itself, what data I can export, how far back to look, and what I want to do with the answer. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to define a normal cycle time before you see any data, so the flagged stages are outliers measured against your own baseline.

items: Where timestamp data lives and whether it exports cleanly.
What counts as a "stage" in your tools.
How far back to look, long enough to be representative, not so long it spans a process that's since changed.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your ticket or task tracker (Jira, Asana, Linear, monday.com), a shared spreadsheet if there's no formal tracker, and your communication tool if bottlenecks show up in thread delays. The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real export, every stage included. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Analyze [X weeks/months] of ticket data from [Jira/Asana/Linear] to find where work stalls in our [process name] process and rank the worst offenders.

Context: [Paste your ticket export: created date, stage, assignee, closed date, for every item.] Process stages in order: [list them]. Normal cycle time is roughly [X days].

Rules:
- Calculate time-in-stage for every item, not just total cycle time.
- Flag any stage where median hold time exceeds [X days].
- Separate rework loops (items that bounced backward) from items that just sat.
- Don't recommend headcount changes, only process fixes.
- Output: a ranked table of stages by hold time, a one-paragraph diagnosis of the worst stage, and 3 next steps.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: separating rework loops from items that just sat keeps a slow-but-correct approval stage from getting flagged the same way as a stage where work is genuinely stuck.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every stage measured, rework separated from hold time, no headcount recommendations?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong (the threshold's too aggressive, a stage got miscounted) and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Re-run it monthly and diff against the last run to show trend.
Feed the flagged bottleneck into the SOP generator blueprint to document a fix.
Build a simple dashboard instead of a static report.
Flag when a bottleneck correlates with a specific person rather than the process, and stop there.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each bottleneck analysis, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, stages flagged, worst offender, hold time, and what threshold I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a shifting bottleneck visible across runs instead of looking new every time.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few runs straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that keeps failing is a skill candidate. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. Timestamps lie when people [batch](#tooltip-batch-api)-update status at day's end, so treat any finding as a hypothesis to check against real examples. A stage that's slow because it's genuinely hard, a real approval, isn't a bottleneck to automate away.
